title: Giving clear instructions

accuracy.evidence: Checked on 25 Nov 2026 against DfE Development Matters (2021) Reception Communication and Language ('use talk to help work out problems and organise thinking and activities, and to explain how things work'), the EYFS Statutory Framework (2024) Early Learning Goal Speaking (offer explanations, full sentences), Talk for Writing guidance on orally rehearsing 'how to' texts in Reception, and English Appendix 2 (a command uses the imperative). Every instruction the lab accepts starts with an imperative verb and names the thing and the place; the four sandwich steps are in the only order that works; the 'get ready' list is exactly what the steps use; a spoon spreads the jam so no knife is shown at age 4-5. The adult text keeps 'bossy verb' as the classroom name for an imperative and says commands are written later, in Year 2.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips reported for young children's spoken instructions (Lloyd, Boada and Forns 1992 on referential communication; Talk for Writing notes on vague 'it' and 'there'): starting with a like, a fact or a question (step 1 prediction, 'like', 'fact', 'ask' and 'story' feedback, the robot waits or does nothing); vague words that make the listener guess (step 3 prediction, the robot puts bread on its head, the whole jar on the bread, bread on the floor; 'guess' and 'exact' slips); getting ready the wrong things ('need' slip, ball, shoe, teddy, crayon refused); muddled order (step 4 prediction, jam on an empty plate, a top with no jam inside; 'order' slip); giving up instead of fixing ('fix' slip).

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanism is a literal-minded robot listener whose result is computed from the words chosen: a scene renders the sandwich state plus a specific muddle for each wrong instruction (waiting with a question mark, bread on its head, the jar on the bread, jam on the plate, top with no jam, bread on the floor), and the build step parses a doing word + thing + place into what the robot does and names which part to change. It is not flagtwo (following two spoken steps), flagpicstory (ordering story cards) or flagkinds (classifying written sentences); the gate measured under 30% source overlap with every flag_*.js.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child finds each rule by watching the robot: a question makes it stand with a question mark until a doing word arrives; vague cards produce a visible muddle before the strip says what was missing (what, where, how much); tapping 'Spread jam on it' first smears jam on an empty plate, so the need for bread first is seen, not told; in the build step 'Put the bread on the floor' makes the robot do exactly that and the strip says 'Change the place', so the child learns each part of an instruction carries meaning.

predictions.evidence: Three committed predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'Which one tells the robot what to do?' (I like bread); 'You say "Put it there." What will the robot do?' (put the bread on the plate, as if it could guess); 'Can the steps go in any order?' (yes). Tasks cannot complete until a prediction is locked, and the done message names the child's prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Eight challenge questions; each wrong option carries a tagged slip with its own message: 'like' (says what you like, not what to do), 'ask' (a question makes the robot wait), 'guess' (a robot cannot guess, say what and where), 'need' (get ready only what the steps use), 'order' (bread first, jam next, top, eat last), 'exact' ('Put jam on' does not say how much or where), 'fix' (find the step and fix the words).

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use very short sentences and everyday words for ages 4-5 (doing word, get ready, what and where), with the instructions themselves as examples; validate_lessons.py passed both readability limits. Lab strips are short, card words are 2 to 7 words in large bold type, and the scene carries the meaning for children who cannot yet read, so a grown-up can read the cards aloud.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one rule (doing word first; get ready; say what and where; order and fixing). Adult paragraphs give the EYFS framework and key words, why giving instructions is harder than following them, the named mistakes, and what each lab step does. The content gate found no filler phrases and under 12% overlap with any lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 screenshots in dark and light themes, including every wrong-answer state: the robot scene sits above big full-width answer cards (three stacked cards in step 1, two side by side in step 3, a 2 by 2 grid of step cards, a 4 by 2 grid of things to get ready), the build step's tiles fill three rows with two or three tiles each and at least 60 px tall, the red or green feedback lines stay at three lines or fewer, and nothing clips the canvas edge.

accessibility.evidence: The fig carries the young class (larger tap targets) and every canvas card has a button twin with a descriptive aria-label ('Tell the robot: Put the bread on the plate.', 'We need: Spoon', 'Say: Put it there.', 'Next step: Spread jam on it.', 'Choose: on the plate'). The canvas aria-label updates with every robot result, challenge feedback is a polite live region, and walk.cjs ran axe WCAG 2.1 AA in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13 with no violations.

sources: DfE Development Matters (2021), Communication and Language, Reception (gov.uk)
DfE Statutory Framework for the Early Years Foundation Stage (2024), ELG Speaking
DfE National Curriculum in England: English Appendix 2, Year 2 (command sentences)
Corbett and Strong, Talk for Writing in the Early Years (instructions: oral rehearsal of 'how to' texts)
Lloyd, Boada and Forns (1992), New directions in referential communication research, British Journal of Developmental Psychology 10(4)
